scope: Complete source-bound Śrīdhara commentary for Canto 11 Chapter 1, verses 11.1.2–11.1.3.

entries.sanskrit: एतद् विवृणोति---ये कोपिता इति । सपत्नैर् दुर्योधनादिभिः कोपिताः कोपं कारिताः । सुबहु यथा भवति, तथा बहु-वारान् इत्य् अर्थः । तद् एवाह---दुर्द्यूत-हेलन-कच-ग्रहणादिभिर् इति । दुर्द्यूतं कपट-द्यूतम्, हेलनम् अवज्ञा, कच-ग्रहणं दुःशासनेन द्रौपद्याः केशाकर्षणम्, एतान्य् आदिर् येषां [गर]{।मर्क्}-दान-जतु-गृह-दाहादीनां तैः कृत्वा, ये कोपिताः, तान् पाण्डु-सुतान् निमित्तं कृत्वा इतरेतरत उभयोः पक्षयोः समेतान् मिलितान् नृपान् हत्वा क्षितेर् भारं निरहरज् जहार । यद् वा, ये कोपिताः, यैश् च कोपिताः, तान् इतरेतरतः परस्परं निमित्तं कृत्वेत्य् अन्वयः । ये तावत् प्रकट-दैत्याः पूतनादयस् तान् स्वयम् एव हतवान् । ये तु दैत्या बान्धव-च्छद्मना स्थिताः, तान् परस्परं निमित्तं विधाय हत्वा भू-भारम् अपाकृतवान् इत्य् अर्थः ॥२॥
word_for_word: with the words beginning ‘those who were angered’
by crooked dice-play, insult, hair-seizing, and the like
those of which these are the first examples
the witness contains a corrupt word before ‘giving’; likely refers to administration of poison, not silently emended
of such acts as burning the lac house
having made the occasion or instrument
he removed; he took away (the witness has the form निरहरज्)
and those by whom they were angered
the grammatical construction is ‘having made [them] the mutual occasion’
those demons who were openly manifest
having made them instruments against one another
entries.literal_english: This expands the preceding verse, beginning ‘those who were angered.’ ‘Angered by rivals’ means made angry by Duryodhana and others, repeatedly, as ‘very much’ indicates. The ways are crooked gambling, contempt, and seizing Draupadī’s hair by Duḥśāsana, along with acts such as the lac-house fire; one word in the witness before ‘giving’ is corrupt and is not silently restored. Making the enraged sons of Pāṇḍu the occasion, he killed the kings assembled on both sides and removed the earth’s burden. Alternatively, the grammatical construction is that the enraged and those who enraged them were made the mutual occasion. Demons manifest openly, such as Pūtanā, he killed himself; demons disguised as relatives he caused to kill one another, thereby removing the earth’s burden.
entries.note: The Sanskrit witness contains [गर]{।मर्क्}-दान and the irregular form निरहरज्. Neither is silently normalized. The alternative syntactic interpretation is retained.

entries.sanskrit: अपि च, भू-भारेत्य्-आदि । अन्याश् च भुवो भार-भूता राज-पृतना राज्ञां पृतनाः सेनाः, राज्ञस् तेषां पृतनाश् चेति वा, स्व-बाहुभिर् गुप्तैः परिरक्षितैर् यदुभिर् विवाहादि-च्छलेन निरस्य हत्वा । बाहुभिर् इति बहु-वचनं, वस्तुतश् चतुर्-भुजाभिप्रायेण । नन्व् एवं कृष्णश् चिकीर्षतीति ज्ञात्वा कथं तस्मै यादवा न द्रुह्यन्ति स्म ? तत्राह---अप्रमेयः प्रमातुम् अशक्यः । चिन्ताम् आह---मन्य इति । नन्व् इति वितर्के । अवनेर् भूमेर् भारो यद्यपि लोक-प्रतीत्या गतस् तथाप्य् अहम् अगतम् एव मन्ये । हि निश्चितम् । यद् यस्माद् अविषह्यं सोढुम् अशक्यम् । यादवं कुलम् इत्य् अनेनैव स्व-वंशत्वत् स्वयं हननम् अनुचितम् इति सूचितम् ॥३॥
word_for_word: who constituted a burden on the earth
the armies, meaning the forces, of kings
राज्ञः तेषां पृतनाः च इति वा
or the kings and their armies
under the pretext of marriages and similar occasions
with the four-armed form in mind
knowing that Kṛṣṇa intended to act thus
did the Yadus not become hostile to him?
although it has gone according to common perception
nevertheless I consider it not gone at all
because it is his own lineage
entries.literal_english: Further, with the verse beginning ‘earth’s burden,’ the royal armies that were a burden on the earth may mean the forces of kings, or both the kings and their forces. Kṛṣṇa cleared these away, killing them through the Yadus whom he protected like his own arms, under the pretext of marriages and similar events. The plural ‘arms’ in truth alludes to his four arms. But if the Yadus knew Kṛṣṇa intended this, why did they not turn against him? ‘Immeasurable’ answers: he cannot be comprehended. His thought is introduced by ‘I think’; ‘nanu’ expresses deliberation. Though people perceive the earth’s burden as removed, he considers it not removed, because the Yadu dynasty remains unbearable. Saying ‘the Yadu family’ suggests that personally killing them would be improper because they are his own kin.
entries.note: The Sanskrit gives two syntactic possibilities for rāja-pṛtanā; both are preserved. The source does not call the following Jīva commentary Śrīdhara’s.
